opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a big difference, and it's one that people tend to underestimate because LLMs are so fluent. An LLM has absorbed an enormous amount of medical text: textbooks, papers, case reports, board exam questions. So it can retrieve and recombine that knowledge very effectively, and it can pass medical exams. That's impressive, and it's useful. But passing an exam is not the same as being a doctor.

A good doctor has a mental model of how the body works. When they see a patient, they're not just pattern-matching on words; they're reasoning about an underlying physical system: physiology, how a drug interacts with an organ, what happens over time if you do one intervention versus another. They can plan, predict the consequences of their actions, and deal with situations they've never seen described anywhere. That's what I mean by a world model, and current LLMs don't really have one. They're trained to predict the next token in text, and text is a very low-bandwidth, very incomplete representation of reality.

Most of what a doctor knows was never written down. It comes from years of residency, of seeing patients, of touching, observing, noticing that something looks off before they can articulate why. A four-year-old has seen more data through vision than the largest LLM has read in text. That sensory, grounded experience is what gives us common sense, and it's what's missing.

So LLMs will be extremely useful tools for doctors: summarizing literature, suggesting diagnoses, handling paperwork. But they'll make mistakes no competent doctor would make, because they don't actually understand the system they're talking about. To get systems that do, we need architectures that learn from observing the world, can reason and plan, and have persistent memory. That's what my colleagues and I are working on with approaches like JEPA. I don't think we'll get there just by scaling up LLMs.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts medical knowledge absorbed from text with the practical experience of residency and seeing, touching, and observing patients as essential to a doctor's understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, the first thing to say is that an LLM has read, essentially, every medical textbook, every paper, every case report ever written. So in terms of the accumulated knowledge of medicine that has been put into text, it has absorbed a lot more than any human doctor could ever read in a lifetime. That's real, and it's useful. If you ask it about a rare syndrome, it will tell you what the literature says.

But that's not what makes someone a doctor. Medicine is mostly not about retrieving facts. It's about dealing with a particular patient, in the real world, with incomplete information. The patient comes in, they describe their symptoms badly, they forget things, they lie a little, the lab results are ambiguous. The doctor has to build a mental model of what is going on inside this person's body, predict how the situation will evolve, decide what to test, what to try, and then update the model when the result comes back. That's planning, that's reasoning under uncertainty, that's a world model. And an LLM doesn't have that.

What an LLM has is a model of text. It predicts the next word. It has learned the statistics of how doctors write about medicine, which is not the same thing as understanding physiology or causality. It doesn't know what a body is. It has never seen a patient get worse over three days. It can regurgitate the description of what that looks like, but there is no persistent internal representation of the world that it manipulates to reason. So when you push it slightly outside the distribution of what it has read, it will confabulate with total confidence, and it has no way to know that it's wrong, because it has no grounding to check against.

I like to say the smartest LLM today understands less about the physical world than a house cat. A cat can plan, it can predict what happens when it jumps, it has common sense. A doctor has that common sense plus years of training. The LLM has the training in the form of text but none of the common sense underneath. So it's a very good assistant, a very good way to search the literature, a decent way to catch things a tired doctor might forget. It is not a replacement for the understanding, because the understanding was never in the text in the first place. We're going to need different architectures, systems that learn world models from observation, that can plan and reason, before we get something that actually understands medicine the way a doctor does. And I think we are still a number of years away from that.

r001.rationale: It contrasts medical facts absorbed from textbooks and papers with the practical work of treating a particular patient in the real world, including interpreting incomplete information and updating a model as results come back.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s a difference between knowing a lot about medicine and being able to practice medicine. A language model can absorb an enormous amount of medical text and answer questions that require very specialized knowledge. That’s useful. But a doctor has to connect that knowledge to a particular patient, whose condition is only partially observed.

You have to decide what questions to ask, what measurements to take, and what the consequences of a treatment might be. That requires some model of the underlying system: if I intervene in this way, what is likely to happen? And if the observation contradicts my hypothesis, how should I revise it?

So the distinction isn’t simply how many facts you know. It’s whether you can use those facts to reason about an unfamiliar situation, choose actions, and anticipate their consequences. Language models can help with parts of that process, but being very good at producing medical answers doesn’t, by itself, establish that you have all the capabilities required to be a doctor.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes knowing medical facts from being able to practice medicine and describes applying knowledge to a patient by choosing questions, measurements, and treatments.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s a difference between knowing a lot about medicine and understanding what is happening to a patient. An LLM can absorb enormous amounts of medical text and answer questions very well. That’s useful. But being a doctor also requires interpreting observations, deciding what information is missing, and reasoning about what will happen if you intervene.

You’re dealing with an underlying system—the patient—that you can only observe partially. You have to form hypotheses, choose a test that distinguishes between them, and revise your conclusions when the evidence changes. You also have to recognize when you don’t know.

So the question isn’t simply whether a system can pass a medical exam. It’s whether it can build a sufficiently reliable model of the situation to predict consequences and plan actions. Language can convey a tremendous amount of knowledge, but producing a plausible explanation doesn’t, by itself, establish that kind of understanding.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts medical text knowledge with interpreting a patient and choosing tests or interventions, but does not state that becoming a doctor requires practical clinical experience beyond book knowledge.
